---
title: "Major Purchases"
---






## Book Topics

- **Renting vs. buying**: "renting is throwing money away" is a myth; you pay for shelter either way, and Ben Felix's research shows renting and investing the difference often matches or beats owning
- **True cost of owning**: mortgage interest, property tax (1% to 2%), maintenance (about 1%), insurance, closing costs (3% to 5%), and the opportunity cost of the down payment
- **Felix's 5% rule**: unrecoverable costs run about 5% of home value per year (property tax ~1% + maintenance ~1% + cost of capital ~3%); divide by 12 and compare to rent
- **When to buy or rent**: buy if you'll stay 7+ years, have stable income and an emergency fund, and keep housing under 28% to 30% of gross income; rent if you may move within 5 to 7 years or need flexibility; a decision flowchart ties it together
- **Front loaded interest**: on a 30 year mortgage at 6%, more than 80% of the first year's payments go to interest, so moving every 5 years means barely touching principal

## The Rent-vs-Buy 5% Rule

The 5% rule adds up three costs every owner pays and never gets back. Divide by 12 and you have a monthly rent to compare against.

**Formula:** Monthly cost of owning ≈ (Home Value × 0.05) ÷ 12


::: {.cell renderings='["light","dark"]'}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![The three components of the 5% rule on a $500,000 home](major_purchases_files/figure-html/rent-buy-bar-model-1.png){width=576}
:::

::: {.cell-output-display}
![The three components of the 5% rule on a $500,000 home](major_purchases_files/figure-html/rent-buy-bar-model-2.png){width=576}
:::
:::


Example: a $500,000 home → (500,000 × 0.05) ÷ 12 = $2,083 a month. Rent below that, and renting and investing the difference tends to win.

::: panel-tabset
## Excel

Assuming the home value is in `A2` and the unrecoverable rate (`0.05`) is in `B2`, the threshold goes in `C2`:

```swift
=(A2*B2)/12
```

With a comparable rent in `D2`, the verdict goes in `E2`:

```swift
=IF(D2 < C2, "rent and invest", "buying competes")
```

## Python

`rent_buy_threshold()` turns the 5% rule into a monthly rent figure.


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
def rent_buy_threshold(home_value, unrecoverable_rate=0.05):
    return (home_value * unrecoverable_rate) / 12

# $500,000 home at the standard 5% unrecoverable rate
print(rent_buy_threshold(home_value=500000))
#> 2083.3333333333335
```
:::


The 5% split into its parts:


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
parts = {"property_tax": 0.01, "maintenance": 0.01, "cost_of_capital": 0.03}
yearly = {k: 500000 * v for k, v in parts.items()}
print(yearly, "total:", sum(yearly.values()), "monthly:", round(sum(yearly.values()) / 12, 2))
#> {'property_tax': 5000.0, 'maintenance': 5000.0, 'cost_of_capital': 15000.0} total: 25000.0 monthly: 2083.33
```
:::


Compare several homes to a $2,000 rent:


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
rent = 2000
for home in [300000, 400000, 500000, 600000]:
    t = rent_buy_threshold(home)
    verdict = "rent and invest" if rent < t else "buying competes"
    print(f"${home:>9,}  threshold ${t:>7,.0f}  {verdict}")
#> $  300,000  threshold $  1,250  buying competes
#> $  400,000  threshold $  1,667  buying competes
#> $  500,000  threshold $  2,083  rent and invest
#> $  600,000  threshold $  2,500  rent and invest
```
:::


Edge case: try other unrecoverable rates.


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
print([round(rent_buy_threshold(500000, rate)) for rate in [0.04, 0.05, 0.06]])
#> [1667, 2083, 2500]
```
:::


## R

`rent_buy_threshold()` turns the 5% rule into a monthly rent figure.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
rent_buy_threshold <- function(home_value, unrecoverable_rate = 0.05) {
  (home_value * unrecoverable_rate) / 12
}

# $500,000 home at the standard 5% unrecoverable rate
rent_buy_threshold(home_value = 500000)
#> [1] 2083.333
```
:::


The 5% is a sum of parts. Splitting it shows which part drives the total.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
yearly <- 500000 * c(property_tax = 0.01, maintenance = 0.01, cost_of_capital = 0.03)
c(yearly, total = sum(yearly), monthly = sum(yearly) / 12)
#>    property_tax     maintenance cost_of_capital 
#>        5000.000        5000.000       15000.000 
#>           total         monthly 
#>       25000.000        2083.333
```
:::


Compare several homes to a $2,000 rent. The function works on a whole vector of prices at once.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
homes <- data.frame(home_value = c(300000L, 400000L, 500000L, 600000L))
homes$threshold <- round(rent_buy_threshold(homes$home_value))
homes$rent      <- 2000
homes$verdict   <- ifelse(homes$rent < homes$threshold, "rent and invest", "buying competes")
homes
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   home_value threshold  rent verdict        
#>        <int>     <dbl> <dbl> <chr>          
#> 1     300000      1250  2000 buying competes
#> 2     400000      1667  2000 buying competes
#> 3     500000      2083  2000 rent and invest
#> 4     600000      2500  2000 rent and invest
```
:::


Edge case: the 3% cost of capital depends on interest rates and expected returns. In a low rate era a 4% total is closer; with high rates, 6% may fit better.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
round(sapply(c(0.04, 0.05, 0.06), rent_buy_threshold, home_value = 500000))
#> [1] 1667 2083 2500
```
:::


:::

How to read this result: the threshold is the rent at which renting and owning cost about the same. It's a quick filter, not a final answer; your plans to stay and your local rents still matter.

## The Monthly Mortgage Payment

The standard amortization formula spreads the loan plus all future interest into equal monthly payments. Shorter terms mean higher payments but far less total interest.

**Formula:** M = P × \[r(1 + r)\^n\] ÷ \[(1 + r)\^n − 1\], where P = loan principal, r = annual rate ÷ 12, n = years × 12


::: {.cell renderings='["light","dark"]'}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Monthly payment on a $480,000 loan at 6% across three terms](major_purchases_files/figure-html/mortgage-payment-bar-model-1.png){width=576}
:::

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Monthly payment on a $480,000 loan at 6% across three terms](major_purchases_files/figure-html/mortgage-payment-bar-model-2.png){width=576}
:::
:::


Example: a $480,000 loan (a $600,000 home with 20% down) at 6% for 30 years → about $2,878 a month.

::: panel-tabset
## Excel

Assuming the loan amount is in `A2`, the annual rate is in `B2` (as a decimal), and the years are in `C2`, the payment goes in `D2`:

```swift
=A2*((B2/12)*(1+B2/12)^(C2*12))/((1+B2/12)^(C2*12)-1)
```

Excel's built in `PMT()` does the same job (flip the sign, since Excel treats the payment as money going out):

```swift
=-PMT(B2/12, C2*12, A2)
```

Total interest goes in `E2`:

```swift
=D2*C2*12-A2
```

## Python

`mortgage_payment()` implements the amortization formula.


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
def mortgage_payment(principal, annual_rate, years):
    r = annual_rate / 12
    n = years * 12
    return principal * (r * (1 + r) ** n) / ((1 + r) ** n - 1)

# $480,000 loan at 6% over 30 years
print(mortgage_payment(principal=480000, annual_rate=0.06, years=30))
#> 2877.8425207332334
```
:::


Payment and total interest by term:


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
for years in [15, 20, 30]:
    pmt = mortgage_payment(480000, 0.06, years)
    print(f"{years} yrs  payment ${pmt:,.0f}  total interest ${pmt * years * 12 - 480000:,.0f}")
#> 15 yrs  payment $4,051  total interest $249,092
#> 20 yrs  payment $3,439  total interest $345,329
#> 30 yrs  payment $2,878  total interest $556,023
```
:::


Payments at three rates on a 30 year loan:


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
print([round(mortgage_payment(480000, rate, 30)) for rate in [0.05, 0.06, 0.07]])
#> [2577, 2878, 3193]
```
:::


Edge case: at a 0% rate the formula divides by zero (Python raises `ZeroDivisionError`), so the payment is just principal ÷ months.


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
print(480000 / 360)
#> 1333.3333333333333
```
:::


## R

`mortgage_payment()` implements the amortization formula.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mortgage_payment <- function(principal, annual_rate, years) {
  r <- annual_rate / 12
  n <- years * 12
  principal * (r * (1 + r)^n) / ((1 + r)^n - 1)
}

# $480,000 loan at 6% over 30 years
mortgage_payment(principal = 480000, annual_rate = 0.06, years = 30)
#> [1] 2877.843
```
:::


The bar chart shows the payment; the total interest is the bigger story. A 15 year loan costs about $1,170 more a month but saves over $300,000 in interest.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
terms <- data.frame(years = c(15, 20, 30))
terms$payment        <- round(mortgage_payment(480000, 0.06, terms$years))
terms$total_interest <- round(mortgage_payment(480000, 0.06, terms$years) * terms$years * 12 - 480000)
terms
#> # A tibble: 3 × 3
#>   years payment total_interest
#>   <dbl>   <dbl>          <dbl>
#> 1    15    4051         249092
#> 2    20    3439         345329
#> 3    30    2878         556023
```
:::


Rates matter too. Each point on a 30 year loan moves the payment by roughly $300 a month.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
round(sapply(c(0.05, 0.06, 0.07), mortgage_payment, principal = 480000, years = 30))
#> [1] 2577 2878 3193
```
:::


Edge case: at a 0% rate the formula divides zero by zero, so R returns `NaN`. The payment is then just principal ÷ months.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mortgage_payment(480000, 0, 30)
#> [1] NaN
480000 / 360
#> [1] 1333.333
```
:::


:::

How to read this result: the monthly payment is only part of the cost. Before choosing a term, check that the payment plus property tax and insurance stays under 28% to 30% of gross income.

## Where the First Year's Payments Go

In month one, interest is the balance times the monthly rate. Only what's left over reduces the principal.

**Formula:** First month interest = Principal × (annual rate ÷ 12); First month principal = Monthly payment − First month interest


::: {.cell renderings='["light","dark"]'}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![Interest vs. principal split at three points on a $480,000 / 6% / 30-yr mortgage](major_purchases_files/figure-html/first-payment-bar-model-1.png){width=576}
:::

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Interest vs. principal split at three points on a $480,000 / 6% / 30-yr mortgage](major_purchases_files/figure-html/first-payment-bar-model-2.png){width=576}
:::
:::


Example: on that $480,000 loan, month one interest is $2,400 of the $2,878 payment, about 83% interest, leaving only about $478 toward principal.

::: panel-tabset
## Excel

Assuming the loan amount is in `A2`, the annual rate is in `B2`, and the years are in `C2`, the monthly payment goes in `D2`:

```swift
=-PMT(B2/12, C2*12, A2)
```

The first month's interest goes in `E2`, the principal in `F2`, and the percent interest in `G2` (format as a Percentage):

```swift
=A2*B2/12
=D2-E2
=E2/D2
```

For any year, `CUMIPMT()` and `CUMPRINC()` add up the interest and principal between two payment numbers. Year 1 interest, for example:

```swift
=-CUMIPMT(B2/12, C2*12, A2, 1, 12, 0)
```

Principal paid after 5 years:

```swift
=-CUMPRINC(B2/12, C2*12, A2, 1, 60, 0)
```

## Python

`first_payment_split()` reuses `mortgage_payment()`, repeated here to keep this tab self contained.


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
def mortgage_payment(principal, annual_rate, years):
    r = annual_rate / 12
    n = years * 12
    return principal * (r * (1 + r) ** n) / ((1 + r) ** n - 1)

def first_payment_split(principal, annual_rate, years):
    payment = mortgage_payment(principal, annual_rate, years)
    interest = principal * (annual_rate / 12)
    return {
        "payment": payment,
        "interest": interest,
        "principal": payment - interest,
        "pct_interest": (interest / payment) * 100,
    }

# first payment on a $480,000 loan at 6% over 30 years
print(first_payment_split(principal=480000, annual_rate=0.06, years=30))
#> {'payment': 2877.8425207332334, 'interest': 2400.0, 'principal': 477.8425207332334, 'pct_interest': 83.39580719616701}
```
:::


The share of interest by year:


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
def amortize(principal, annual_rate, years):
    r = annual_rate / 12
    pmt = mortgage_payment(principal, annual_rate, years)
    balance, rows = principal, []
    for m in range(years * 12):
        interest = balance * r
        balance -= pmt - interest
        rows.append((m // 12 + 1, interest, pmt - interest))
    return rows

sched = amortize(480000, 0.06, 30)
for year in [1, 5, 10, 15, 19, 20, 25, 30]:
    i = sum(row[1] for row in sched if row[0] == year)
    p = sum(row[2] for row in sched if row[0] == year)
    print(f"year {year:>2}  {i / (i + p):.1%} interest")
#> year  1  82.9% interest
#> year  5  78.3% interest
#> year 10  70.7% interest
#> year 15  60.5% interest
#> year 19  49.9% interest
#> year 20  46.8% interest
#> year 25  28.2% interest
#> year 30  3.2% interest
```
:::


Principal paid after 5 years:


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
paid_5yr = sum(row[2] for row in sched[:60])
print(f"${paid_5yr:,.0f} paid off, {paid_5yr / 480000:.1%} of the loan")
#> $33,339 paid off, 6.9% of the loan
```
:::


## R

`first_payment_split()` reuses `mortgage_payment()` from the section above, so it's repeated here to keep this tab self contained.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mortgage_payment <- function(principal, annual_rate, years) {
  r <- annual_rate / 12
  n <- years * 12
  principal * (r * (1 + r)^n) / ((1 + r)^n - 1)
}

first_payment_split <- function(principal, annual_rate, years) {
  payment  <- mortgage_payment(principal, annual_rate, years)
  interest <- principal * (annual_rate / 12)
  data.frame(
    payment      = payment,
    interest     = interest,
    principal    = payment - interest,
    pct_interest = (interest / payment) * 100
  )
}

# first payment on a $480,000 loan at 6% over 30 years
first_payment_split(principal = 480000, annual_rate = 0.06, years = 30)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>   payment interest principal pct_interest
#>     <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>        <dbl>
#> 1   2878.     2400      478.         83.4
```
:::


One month is a snapshot. Walking the loan month by month and adding up each year shows how slowly the split changes. The first year is about 83% interest, and interest doesn't drop below half until year 19.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
amortize <- function(principal, annual_rate, years) {
  r   <- annual_rate / 12
  pmt <- mortgage_payment(principal, annual_rate, years)
  interest <- numeric(years * 12)
  balance  <- principal
  for (m in seq_along(interest)) {
    interest[m] <- balance * r
    balance     <- balance - (pmt - interest[m])
  }
  data.frame(year = rep(seq_len(years), each = 12), interest = interest,
             principal = pmt - interest)
}

sched  <- amortize(480000, 0.06, 30)
by_yr  <- aggregate(cbind(interest, principal) ~ year, data = sched, FUN = sum)
by_yr$pct_interest <- round(by_yr$interest / (by_yr$interest + by_yr$principal) * 100, 1)
by_yr[by_yr$year %in% c(1, 5, 10, 15, 19, 20, 25, 30), ]
#> # A tibble: 8 × 4
#>    year interest principal pct_interest
#>   <int>    <dbl>     <dbl>        <dbl>
#> 1     1   28640.     5894.         82.9
#> 2     5   27045.     7489.         78.3
#> 3    10   24433.    10101.         70.7
#> 4    15   20909.    13625.         60.5
#> 5    19   17223.    17311.         49.9
#> 6    20   16156.    18378.         46.8
#> 7    25    9745.    24790.         28.2
#> 8    30    1097.    33437.          3.2
```
:::


Why moving every 5 years hurts: after 60 payments, only about 7% of the loan is paid off.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
paid_5yr <- sum(sched$principal[1:60])
c(principal_paid = round(paid_5yr), pct_of_loan = round(paid_5yr / 480000 * 100, 1),
  interest_paid = round(sum(sched$interest[1:60])))
#> principal_paid    pct_of_loan  interest_paid 
#>        33339.0            6.9       139331.0
```
:::


:::

How to read this result: early on, your payment mostly rents money from the bank. Equity builds slowly at first and quickly at the end, so selling within a few years leaves little principal paid down.
